title: The Smell of Soup and the Sound of Money
summary: One chilly winter afternoon in the bustling marketplace of Aksehir, a poor, shivering traveler walked past the steaming kitchen of a wealthy restaurant. The tavern master was boili...
keywords: the smell of soup and the sound of money
full_text:
One chilly winter afternoon in the bustling marketplace of Aksehir, a poor, shivering traveler walked past the steaming kitchen of a wealthy restaurant. The tavern master was boiling a giant cauldron of fragrant lamb broth seasoned with garlic, cinnamon, and cumin.

The penniless traveler pulled a dry crust of barley bread from his pocket and held it over the fragrant steam rising from the pot. He turned the bread around, inhaled the mouth-watering aroma deeply, and ate his softened crust with immense satisfaction.

Just as the poor man was about to walk away, the greedy restaurant owner leaped out of the shop, seized him by the collar, and roared: "Pay me five copper coins this instant!"

"For what, sir?" gasped the bewildered traveler. "I took not a single drop of your soup!"

"You nourished your bread with my rich steam!" barked the merchant. "The aroma belongs to my cauldron, and you have consumed its goodness!"

A crowd gathered, arguing loudly, when Mulla Nasruddin arrived riding his little gray donkey. Hearing the dispute, Nasruddin stroked his beard solemnly and announced: "Step aside, citizens! I shall adjudicate this case of high culinary jurisprudence!"

Nasruddin turned to the restaurant owner: "Is it true that this man ate the steam of your soup?"
"It is entirely true, Mulla!" cried the shopkeeper eagerly. "And steam costs good money to produce!"

Nasruddin reached deep into his pocket and pulled out five copper coins. He cupped the coins tightly inside his hands and shook them vigorously right next to the tavern master's ear: Jingle, jingle, clink!

"Do you hear that sound, tavern master?" asked Nasruddin with a serious frown.
"Of course I hear it, Mulla!" replied the greedy man. "What of it?"

"The judgment is settled!" proclaimed Nasruddin, pocketing the coins once more. "The sound of money pays in full for the smell of soup. Case dismissed!"

The crowd burst into uproarious laughter, while the greedy merchant slunk back into his shop, thoroughly outwitted by the Mulla's impeccable justice.
moral: A frivolous claim based on thin air deserves to be paid with nothing more than sound.

title: Who Stole the Smell?
summary: A baker who was notorious throughout the province for his extreme stinginess noticed that townsfolk often paused outside his bakery window in the early morning simply to enjoy the...
full_text:
A baker who was notorious throughout the province for his extreme stinginess noticed that townsfolk often paused outside his bakery window in the early morning simply to enjoy the delicious fragrance of fresh baking bread.

Outraged that people were enjoying his merchandise without paying, the baker posted an armed guard at his door and brought a formal lawsuit before the town magistrate, charging thirty citizens with "stealing the fragrance of fresh rye."

The magistrate, completely baffled by the absurd complaint, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to give his opinion as the resident scholar.

Nasruddin listened with grave dignity. Then he asked the baker: "How much has your bakery's fragrance diminished because these poor people inhaled it?"

"Why, it hasn't diminished at all," stammered the baker. "The street still smells just as delicious!"

"Then by the ancient law of balance," declared Nasruddin, "the defendants must pay you with an equal portion of their shadows! Tomorrow at noon, when the sun is at its zenith, all thirty citizens shall stand in front of your shop window and allow you to look at their shadows for ten minutes. If you can bake bread with their shadows, you may keep them!"

The entire town square erupted in cheers, and the baker tore down his ridiculous lawsuit in utter embarrassment.
moral: Trying to hoard what nature gives freely makes one an object of public ridicule.

title: The Donkey and the Book
summary: Timur the Lame, the fierce conqueror, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to his grand pavilion. "Mulla," boomed the tyrant, "they say you are a teacher of miraculous wisdom. Can you teach my...
full_text:
Timur the Lame, the fierce conqueror, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to his grand pavilion. "Mulla," boomed the tyrant, "they say you are a teacher of miraculous wisdom. Can you teach my favorite donkey to read the great books of philosophy? If you succeed in ten years, I will grant you a chest of rubies; if you fail, you shall lose your head!"

Nasruddin bowed to the floor: "Sire, it shall be done! I require only ten years and a monthly stipend of gold to conduct the donkey's literary education."

When Nasruddin returned home leading the donkey, his terrified wife wept: "Are you insane, husband? How can an animal learn to read? In ten years you will be executed!"

"Be calm, my dear," smiled Nasruddin with a serene wink. "Ten years is a very long time! Within ten years, either Timur will die, or I will die, or the donkey will die! And in the meantime, we shall live comfortably on the royal stipend!"

Every day, Nasruddin hid grains of barley between the parchment pages of a large book. The donkey quickly learned to flip the pages with his tongue to eat the grains. When Nasruddin brought the donkey before the court, the beast eagerly turned the pages with his muzzle, braying loudly when no more barley was found.

"Look, Your Majesty!" exclaimed Nasruddin proudly. "The donkey has already mastered reading; he has completed chapter three and is now debating the author's logic!" Timur was so amused by the spectacle that he doubled the Mulla's reward.
moral: Flattering despots with impossible promises requires a long horizon and clever strategy.

title: The Lost Key
summary: Late one moonlit evening, several neighbors walking through the town square noticed Mulla Nasruddin down on all fours in the dust beneath a bright street lamp, searching franticall...
full_text:
Late one moonlit evening, several neighbors walking through the town square noticed Mulla Nasruddin down on all fours in the dust beneath a bright street lamp, searching frantically for something.

"What have you lost, Mulla?" asked a friendly neighbor, kneeling down to help him sift through the gravel.

"I have lost the iron key to my front door," replied Nasruddin, wiping sweat from his brow.

The neighbors immediately joined the search. For nearly an hour, five men crawled upon their hands and knees, combing through every pebble beneath the lamp, but not a trace of the key could be found.

Exhausted, one of the neighbors asked: "Mulla, are you absolutely sure you dropped the key here in the square?"

"Oh, no!" answered Nasruddin casually, pointing toward the dark alleyway twenty yards away. "I dropped it inside the dark coal-cellar behind my house!"

The neighbors stared at him in utter disbelief: "Then why in heaven's name are you searching for it out here under the street lamp?"

"Can you not see?" laughed Nasruddin with wide-eyed innocence. "It is pitch black in my cellar, whereas out here under the street lamp, there is plenty of light to see!"

The neighbors groaned, but Sufi masters smiled, knowing Nasruddin had just illustrated how mortals seek truth in the superficial glitter of the world rather than searching the deep, dark caverns of their own hearts.
moral: Searching for answers where it is convenient rather than where the truth was lost is human folly.

title: You Should Have Seen Me Before
summary: A group of strapping young wrestlers gathered in the village square, boasting of their mighty strength. One claimed he could lift an ox; another boasted he could uproot an olive tr...
keywords: you should have seen me before
full_text:
A group of strapping young wrestlers gathered in the village square, boasting of their mighty strength. One claimed he could lift an ox; another boasted he could uproot an olive tree.

Mulla Nasruddin, who was now well past seventy years of age with a snowy white beard and creaking joints, strode into the circle, puffing out his chest.

"You call that strength?" scoffed Nasruddin. "Why, I am just as strong today as I was when I was a fiery youth of twenty!"

The villagers were astonished. "Come now, Mulla!" said an elder. "How can an old man of seventy be as strong as a youth of twenty?"

"I have scientific proof!" declared Nasruddin proudly. "In my backyard stands an enormous stone boulder. When I was twenty years old, I tried with all my might to lift it, and I could not move it an inch. Yesterday morning, I tried with all my might to lift that very same boulder, and I still could not move it an inch! Therefore, my strength is exactly the same!"
moral: Boasting of lost youth only highlights the frailty of present vanity.

title: The Taste of the Same Donkey
summary: A traveling quack physician arrived in the village selling "Miraculous Elixir of Arabian Gazelle," claiming a single drop cured all ailments. He charged ten silver pieces per vial....
keywords: the taste of the same donkey
full_text:
A traveling quack physician arrived in the village selling "Miraculous Elixir of Arabian Gazelle," claiming a single drop cured all ailments. He charged ten silver pieces per vial.

Nasruddin, suspecting a fraud, bought a vial, tasted a drop, and immediately spit it out: "Why, this is nothing but plain ditch water mixed with donkey vinegar!"

The quack became indignant: "How dare an ignorant villager insult imperial medicine! Bring me ten sick men, and I will prove its celestial potency!"

Nasruddin returned with his own wooden jug filled with water from his garden cistern. He had two villagers taste both the quack's potion and his own cistern water. Both villagers agreed that Nasruddin's water tasted much sweeter and fresher.

"You see?" announced Nasruddin to the crowd. "The quack sells sour donkey vinegar in gold vials, while my donkey gives pure spring water for free! Keep your silver coins in your pockets, and drink fresh water from your own wells!"
moral: Blind faith in labels often deceives people into accepting ordinary reality as magic.

title: The Coat Gets Invited
summary: A wealthy nobleman hosted a lavish banquet for the town dignitaries. Mulla Nasruddin, having worked all morning in his dusty vineyard, arrived at the palace in his worn, patched wo...
full_text:
A wealthy nobleman hosted a lavish banquet for the town dignitaries. Mulla Nasruddin, having worked all morning in his dusty vineyard, arrived at the palace in his worn, patched work clothes and mud-spattered boots.

The snobbish servants glanced at his rags and pushed him to the drafty corner near the kitchen door. The host walked past him without a word of greeting, and the waiters served him only cold broth and burnt crusts.

Nasruddin quietly slipped away, hurried home, and washed thoroughly. He put on his most magnificent holiday robe—a flowing kaftan of shimmering scarlet silk embroidered with gold thread and trimmed with luxurious fox fur—and donned a grand turban adorned with a silver brooch.

When he returned to the banquet hall, the servants bowed to the floor, opening the double doors with fanfare. The host rushed forward with open arms, embraced the Mulla, and seated him at the head of the banquet table upon velvet cushions.

Waiters immediately brought platters of roasted partridge, saffron pilaf, roasted almonds, and sweet pistachio halva.

Nasruddin smiled graciously. He picked up a spoonful of rich saffron stew and poured it directly into the sleeve of his silk robe! Then he dipped the fur hem of his kaftan into the almond sauce and rubbed sweet halva over his gold embroidery, murmuring affectionately: "Eat, my fine coat, eat! Enjoy the soup! Feast upon the pilaf!"

The host and guests were flabbergasted: "Mulla, what on earth are you doing? Why are you feeding your clothes?"

Nasruddin wiped his hands calmly and replied: "When I arrived an hour ago in my honest human body, wearing my working clothes, you turned me away into the cold corner. But when this coat arrived, you offered velvet cushions and royal delicacies! Therefore, it is obvious that this feast was prepared not for me, but for my coat! And it is only fair that the coat should enjoy what it has earned!"

The host blushed crimson with shame and apologized profusely, while the guests learned a lifelong lesson about the true worth of character over appearances.
moral: People who judge a man by his fine garments are entertaining clothes, not character.

title: How to Divide the Nuts
summary: Five boys were quarreling bitterly in the orchard over a sack of one hundred walnuts they had gathered. Unable to agree on a fair division, they saw Mulla Nasruddin approaching on...
full_text:
Five boys were quarreling bitterly in the orchard over a sack of one hundred walnuts they had gathered. Unable to agree on a fair division, they saw Mulla Nasruddin approaching on his donkey and ran to him: "O wise Mulla! Please divide these walnuts among us fairly!"

Nasruddin sat down on a boulder and smiled: "Tell me, boys: do you wish me to divide these nuts according to human division, or according to God's division?"

The boys shouted eagerly: "According to God's division, Mulla! God's division must surely be the most perfect and sublime!"

"Very well," said Nasruddin.

He opened the sack. To the first boy, he gave seventy walnuts; to the second boy, he gave fifteen; to the third boy, he gave ten; to the fourth boy, he gave four; and to the fifth boy, he gave only one single wrinkled nut!

The boys were stunned and began to protest loudly: "Mulla! This is completely unfair! One boy got almost everything, and the last boy got almost nothing!"

Nasruddin stroked his beard with a twinkle in his eye: "Did you not ask for God's division? In this world, God gives boundless wealth to one man, a modest living to another, and poverty to a third, testing the generosity of the rich and the patience of the poor! If you had wanted an equal share for everyone, you should have asked for human division!"
moral: Human justice seeks fair equality; divine providence distributes according to mysterious design.

title: The Moon is More Useful
summary: Two philosophers were debating in the tea-house whether the sun or the moon was the greater celestial blessing to humanity. The debate grew heated, with each citing ancient astrono...
full_text:
Two philosophers were debating in the tea-house whether the sun or the moon was the greater celestial blessing to humanity. The debate grew heated, with each citing ancient astronomical charts.

Seeing Mulla Nasruddin sipping his mint tea in the corner, they turned to him: "Tell us, Mulla! As a man of practical wisdom, which is more useful to mankind: the sun or the moon?"

Nasruddin pondered for a moment, stroked his beard, and answered decisively: "The moon is infinitely more useful than the sun!"

The philosophers were surprised: "How do you figure that, Mulla?"

"The reason is obvious to any thinking person!" explained Nasruddin. "The sun shines only during the daytime, when it is already bright and nobody needs light! But the moon shines in the middle of the pitch-black night, when it is dark and we truly need illumination! Therefore, the moon is far superior!"
moral: People often undervalue constant blessings while praising what arrives in moments of darkness.

full_text:

His neighbor ran to him: "What wonderful news has happened, Mulla? Did you find a pot of gold?"

"No!" beamed Nasruddin. "My donkey ran away and fell into a deep ravine, breaking its neck!"

The neighbor stared at him: "Are you mad, Mulla? Why are you thanking heaven that your only donkey is dead?"

"Foolish neighbor!" laughed Nasruddin. "Can you not see the boundless mercy? I am thanking heaven that I was not riding on its back when it fell! Otherwise, I would have broken my neck along with it!"
moral: Finding reasons for gratitude even in misfortune preserves a cheerful spirit.

title: Whose Voice?
summary: A neighbor who was notoriously careless with borrowed tools knocked on Nasruddin's door: "Mulla, lend me your donkey for the afternoon; I must carry timber from the forest."...
full_text:
A neighbor who was notoriously careless with borrowed tools knocked on Nasruddin's door: "Mulla, lend me your donkey for the afternoon; I must carry timber from the forest."

Nasruddin, who knew the neighbor never fed borrowed animals, replied from inside: "I would gladly lend it to you, my dear friend, but alas, my donkey is not here today; my son took it to the neighboring town at dawn."

Just at that moment, the donkey brayed loudly from inside the stable: "Hee-haw! Hee-haw!"

The neighbor became indignant: "Shame on you, Mulla! You tell me the donkey is in the neighboring town, when I can hear it braying with my own ears right inside your stable!"

Nasruddin stepped onto the porch, looking at the neighbor with offended dignity: "My good man! Whom do you choose to believe: an honorable scholar with a gray beard who speaks the truth, or an ignorant donkey?"
moral: Believing an animal's noise over the reasoned word of a friend exposes shallow faith.

title: The Borrowed Pot
summary: Mulla Nasruddin borrowed a large bronze cooking pot from his wealthy, greedy neighbor to prepare a family feast. A week later, he returned the pot, but inside it rested a tiny litt...
full_text:
Mulla Nasruddin borrowed a large bronze cooking pot from his wealthy, greedy neighbor to prepare a family feast. A week later, he returned the pot, but inside it rested a tiny little copper pot.

The neighbor was puzzled: "Mulla, what is this tiny pot doing inside my cauldron?"

"Rejoice, neighbor!" whispered Nasruddin solemnly. "While your pot was in my kitchen, it became pregnant and gave birth to this delightful little child! And since you own the mother, the child belongs to you by law!"

The greedy neighbor laughed to himself, thinking Nasruddin was a simpleton, and happily kept both pots.

A month later, Nasruddin came back and borrowed the big cauldron again. Weeks passed, and Nasruddin did not return it. Finally, the neighbor marched to Nasruddin's house, demanding: "Where is my cooking pot, Mulla?"

Nasruddin wiped away a tear: "Alas, my dear neighbor! I bring you tragic news! Your beloved bronze pot has passed away; it died peacefully in my kitchen yesterday, and I buried it with full honors."

"Are you out of your mind?" screamed the furious neighbor. "How can a bronze cooking pot die?"

"Come now, neighbor," smiled Nasruddin calmly. "You were perfectly willing to believe that your pot could give birth to a baby; why then can you not believe that it can die? Whatever is born must surely one day taste death!"
moral: If you accept an impossible gain based on greed, you must also accept the impossible loss.

title: The Ringing in the Ears
summary: A patient visited Nasruddin complaining of a persistent ringing sound in his left ear....
full_text:
A patient visited Nasruddin complaining of a persistent ringing sound in his left ear.

"Mulla, what mysterious ailment is this?" asked the frightened man.

Nasruddin examined the ear, tapped the man's temple with his pipe, and asked: "Do you have any debts?"

"None at all," replied the man.

"Do you have a wife?" "No." "Do you lend money to relatives?" "Never."

"Then do not worry!" laughed Nasruddin. "The ringing in your ears is simply the sound of your empty pockets jingling in the wind! Borrow some money, get married, and take in three relatives, and you will soon have so many real troubles that you will never hear the ringing again!"
moral: Pretentious medical jargon often masks simple common sense.

title: The Price of a Dream
summary: A miserly merchant brought a poor weaver before the court, shouting: "Last night I dreamed that this pauper broke into my storehouse and stole ten sacks of flour! He must pay me fi...
full_text:
A miserly merchant brought a poor weaver before the court, shouting: "Last night I dreamed that this pauper broke into my storehouse and stole ten sacks of flour! He must pay me fifty silver coins for the loss!"

The town judge was dumbfounded, but Nasruddin stepped forward: "I shall dispense justice!"

Nasruddin placed a polished silver mirror on the table, took fifty silver coins from his purse, and placed them in front of the glass.

He told the merchant: "Look into the mirror, merchant! Do you see those fifty shiny coins reflected in the glass?"

"Yes, Mulla!" said the merchant eagerly.

"Then take the reflection of the coins," ruled Nasruddin. "For an imaginary theft in a dream, an imaginary payment in a mirror is the exact legal price!"
moral: An imaginary injury deserves nothing more than an imaginary compensation.

Tasked by a harsh governor to teach his donkey to read within five years, Nasruddin trained the animal to turn pages with its tongue by spreading barley meal between the leaves of an enormous parchment manuscript.

When the donkey turned the final page and found no grain, it threw back its head and let out a mighty bray.

"Look, Governor!" announced Nasruddin with grave dignity. "The donkey has read through the entire treaty on civil governance, and is now delivering his oral critique of your administration's tax policies!" The governor was so amused that he awarded the Mulla a robe of honor.
moral: True wisdom outlasts mortal threats by applying patience and clever insight.

full_text:
In the dead of night, a burglar broke into Nasruddin's modest cottage. The thief searched under the cot, overturned empty clay jars, and rummaged through the kitchen cupboards, finding not a single valuable item.

Finally, opening the small wooden wardrobe in the corner, the thief was astonished to find Mulla Nasruddin sitting crouched inside, wrapped in a blanket!

"What are you doing inside the wardrobe, old man?" gasped the startled thief.

Nasruddin looked at him with an embarrassed smile: "I saw you searching our house so diligently, and I was so ashamed of our extreme poverty that I hid in here so you wouldn't see how little we have to offer!"
moral: Poverty is no disgrace; owning nothing frees one from fear of robbers.

title: Half Knowledge

full_text:
A haughty grammarian boarded Nasruddin's ferry to cross a turbulent river. During the crossing, the scholar asked sneeringly: "Mulla, have you ever studied Arabic grammar and the rules of prosody?"

"No, sir," replied Nasruddin, pulling steadily at the oars.

"Then half of your life has been completely wasted!" mocked the scholar.

A sudden gust of wind hit the ferry, and the boat began to take in water rapidly. Nasruddin turned to the trembling professor: "Professor, have you ever studied the science of swimming?"

"No, alas, never!" cried the scholar in terror.

"Then your whole life is wasted!" shouted Nasruddin, diving into the current. "For this boat is sinking!"
moral: Academic arrogance is useless when the river of reality rises; practical skill saves life.

title: The Hot Soup and Cold Winter
summary: The village elders bet Nasruddin that he could not spend an entire freezing winter night on the snowy mountain peak without a fire, coat, or blanket. If he survived, they would buy...
keywords: the hot soup and cold winter
full_text:
The village elders bet Nasruddin that he could not spend an entire freezing winter night on the snowy mountain peak without a fire, coat, or blanket. If he survived, they would buy him a grand feast.

Nasruddin accepted the wager, stood on the freezing summit all night, and survived by watching a tiny candle flame flickering in a farmhouse window a mile away.

The next morning, the greedy elders refused to pay: "You warmed yourself by the candle light a mile away! You lost the bet!"

Nasruddin said nothing. He invited them to dinner that evening. The guests arrived hungry, but after two hours, no food appeared. Looking into the kitchen, they saw Nasruddin holding a giant cauldron of soup suspended from the ceiling, with a tiny candle burning on the floor five feet below it!

"Mulla, are you crazy?" shouted the elders. "How can a candle five feet below boil a giant pot?"

title: The Sermon
summary: Mounting the pulpit on Friday, Nasruddin asked the congregation: "Do you know what I am going to speak about today?"...
full_text:
Mounting the pulpit on Friday, Nasruddin asked the congregation: "Do you know what I am going to speak about today?"

"No, Mulla!" replied the crowd.
"If you do not know, I have no desire to waste words on such ignorant people!" said Nasruddin, and he stepped down and went home.

The next Friday, he asked the same question. The people, determined not to be dismissed, replied: "Yes, Mulla, we know!"
"If you already know," said Nasruddin, "there is no need for me to tell you!" And he departed once more.

On the third Friday, the people agreed among themselves: half would answer "Yes" and half would answer "No."

Nasruddin asked: "Do you know what I am going to speak about?"
Half the congregation cried "Yes!" and half cried "No!"

Nasruddin beamed with delight: "Splendid! Then let those who know tell those who do not!" And he walked out into the sunshine.
moral: Teaching that relies on the community to enlighten one another achieves true harmony.

An innkeeper charged Nasruddin five gold pieces for two boiled eggs, arguing: "If those two eggs had hatched into hens, and those hens had laid eggs, in five years they would have produced a flock worth fifty gold pieces!"

Nasruddin accepted the bill, but asked for an hour's delay. He returned with a large bag of roasted barley and began scattering it in the town garden.

The innkeeper asked: "Why are you planting roasted barley, Mulla?"

"To harvest a crop of barley to pay your fifty gold pieces!" replied Nasruddin.

"Can roasted barley sprout?" laughed the innkeeper.

"If boiled eggs can hatch into laying hens," retorted Nasruddin, "roasted barley can surely sprout into golden fields!" The innkeeper dropped the charge in shame.
moral: Confronting greedy speculation with literal absurdity reveals its foolishness.

title: The Cat Ate the Meat
summary: Nasruddin bought three pounds of prime lamb at the bazaar, carried it home, and told his wife: "Prepare a rich meat stew for tonight; I have invited several honored friends."...
full_text:
Nasruddin bought three pounds of prime lamb at the bazaar, carried it home, and told his wife: "Prepare a rich meat stew for tonight; I have invited several honored friends."

While Nasruddin was at the mosque, his wife cooked the delicious stew, but could not resist tasting a piece. One piece led to another, and soon she and her gossiping neighbors had eaten every single scrap of the meat.

When Nasruddin returned with his hungry guests, his wife pretended to weep: "Alas, husband! A catastrophe! While I turned my back, your greedy black cat leaped onto the stove and ate all three pounds of lamb!"

Nasruddin did not raise his voice. He quietly picked up the black cat, carried it to the apothecary's shop next door, and placed it on the merchant's brass scale.

The weights balanced at exactly three pounds!

Nasruddin turned to his blushing wife with a serious frown: "My dear, if this three pounds of flesh on the scale is the cat—then where on earth is the meat? And if this is the meat—then where on earth is the cat?"
moral: Transparent lies crumble before the simplest test of logic.

Nasruddin stroked his beard thoughtfully: "That is simple. Buy a suit of clown's bells, paint your face green, dance on one foot through the bazaar, and tell everyone you are a cabbage!"

"Will that hide me from the Angel of Death?" gasped the merchant.

"Certainly not!" replied Nasruddin. "The Angel of Death will find you just as easily. But at least you will die making people laugh, which is far better than dying of miserable worry!"
moral: Fear of death robs life of joy; living fully in the present is true wisdom.

Nasruddin pocketed the gold and whispered: "The greatest secret is this: never give ten gold dinars to a man who sells words!"

Nasruddin took off his enormous turban, placed it upon the peasant's head, and said: "Here! Now that you are wearing the watermelon turban, read the letter yourself!"
moral: A magnificent turban does not grant the ability to read what is written in gibberish.

title: The Candle in the Window (The Parable of the Stew)
summary: Having survived an entire freezing night on the snowy mountain by watching a candle flame a mile away, Nasruddin was denied his wager by greedy elders who claimed the distant candl...
full_text:
Having survived an entire freezing night on the snowy mountain by watching a candle flame a mile away, Nasruddin was denied his wager by greedy elders who claimed the distant candle had warmed him.

When they arrived at his house for dinner, he showed them a cauldron of stew hanging five feet above a tiny candle on the floor.

"How can that candle cook the stew?" they shouted.

"If it could warm a grown man through a blizzard a mile away," smiled Nasruddin, "it can surely cook stew five feet above it!" The elders bowed in shame and paid the wager.
moral: Those who use absurd excuses to cheat others must taste their own medicine.

title: Nasruddin and Timur
summary: Timur the Conqueror looked into a mirror, saw his scarred face and blind eye, and burst into tears of grief. His courtiers immediately began weeping in sycophantic sympathy....
full_text:
Timur the Conqueror looked into a mirror, saw his scarred face and blind eye, and burst into tears of grief. His courtiers immediately began weeping in sycophantic sympathy.

After two hours, Timur stopped weeping and smiled, and his courtiers instantly dried their eyes. Only Mulla Nasruddin continued to wail at the top of his lungs, tearing his robe.

"Mulla," snapped Timur, "I have stopped weeping; why do you continue to howl?"

"Sire!" sobbed Nasruddin. "You looked into the mirror for a single minute and wept for two hours. I have to look at your face all day long; imagine how much more I must weep!" Timur burst into laughter and rewarded the fearless Mulla.
moral: Clever wit and unflinching presence of mind can disarm even the most ruthless tyrant.

title: The Man Counting Donkeys
summary: Nasruddin bought nine donkeys at the market and rode one of them toward home. Along the road, he counted the animals: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight! Alas! A donke...
full_text:
Nasruddin bought nine donkeys at the market and rode one of them toward home. Along the road, he counted the animals: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight! Alas! A donkey is missing!"

He leaped down from his saddle in panic, searched behind the bushes, and counted again: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine! Ah, it has returned!"

He mounted his donkey again and rode on. After a mile, he counted once more: "Eight again! A demon is stealing my donkeys!"

His wife met him at the gate: "Husband, what is the matter?"

"I bought nine donkeys, but whenever I ride, there are only eight; and whenever I walk, there are nine!"

His wife shook her head: "I see ten donkeys! Nine on four legs, and one on two legs sitting on top of the first!"
moral: People often count all external things while forgetting the vehicle that carries them.

A sudden gust of wind blew Nasruddin's freshly washed linen shirt off the drying line on the second-story balcony, dropping it onto the stone flagstones below.

Nasruddin immediately prostrated himself on the floor, offering prayers of thanksgiving.

His wife was bewildered: "Why are you praying because your shirt fell into the dirt?"

"Can you not see the miracle?" exclaimed Nasruddin. "Thank heaven I was not inside the shirt when it fell! Otherwise, I would have broken all my bones upon the stones!"
moral: A cheerful mind finds reasons for gratitude even in minor accidents.

title: The Chess with the King
summary: The King challenged Nasruddin to a game of chess, boasting that no one in the realm could defeat him....
full_text:
The King challenged Nasruddin to a game of chess, boasting that no one in the realm could defeat him.

Nasruddin played brilliantly, checkmating the monarch in twelve moves. Enraged, the King seized the heavy wooden chessboard and struck Nasruddin across the shoulders with it.

A week later, the King demanded another game. When Nasruddin saw he was about to deliver checkmate again, he quickly leaped under the table with a pillow tied over his head!

"What are you doing under the table?" demanded the King.

"Sire," replied Nasruddin from beneath the cushions, "I am delivering checkmate! But I have prepared my defenses beforehand!" The King laughed and rewarded his wit.
moral: Playing games with tyrants requires losing with grace and winning with discretion.

moral: A seller who praises faults as virtues is an artist of deception.

Nasruddin's wife hid a jar of golden honey on the top shelf, warning him: "Husband, do not touch that jar! It contains lethal poison; a single spoonful will cause sudden death!"

While she was visiting neighbors, Nasruddin pulled down the jar, fetched a loaf of fresh bread, and ate every single drop of the honey.

When his wife returned and found the jar empty, Nasruddin lay on the floor groaning: "Forgive me, wife! I broke your favorite bowl, and was so filled with remorse that I ate the entire jar of poison so I could die in peace! But alas, the poison has not worked yet!"
moral: Cunning warnings often tempt the curious into discovering the sweet truth.

full_text:
Nasruddin was building a brick wall in his garden. After working all day, he found he had exactly two bricks left over.

He spent three hours measuring, digging, and recalculating where to place the two extra bricks.

Finally, his wife called out: "Husband, just toss the two bricks into the garden corner!"

Nasruddin wiped his forehead in admiration: "How marvelous is woman's intellect! I have studied Euclidean geometry for forty years, yet she solved the crisis in two seconds!"
moral: Complicated architectural schemes often stumble over the simplest arithmetic.

A merchant asked Nasruddin to write a letter to a business partner in Damascus. Nasruddin agreed and scribbled two pages of bizarre, jagged lines.

"Now, Mulla," said the merchant, "please give it to the courier."

"No," said Nasruddin, "if this letter is to reach Damascus, you must pay for my travel expenses so I can accompany the letter in person!"

"Why on earth must you go along?" asked the merchant.

"Because my handwriting is so uniquely profound that no human being in Damascus can read it unless I am standing right beside them to explain what it means!"
moral: When skill is lacking, inventive excuses disguise human limitation.

A traveler hired Nasruddin's donkey for a journey across the scorching desert. At midday, with the sun blazing down, the traveler sat down in the shade cast by the donkey's body to rest.

Nasruddin pushed him aside: "This shade is mine! You rented the donkey, but you did not rent its shadow!"

The traveler argued: "Renting the donkey includes whatever shade it casts!"

While the two men wrestled furiously in the sand over the ownership of the shadow, the donkey grew frightened and galloped away into the wilderness, leaving both men stranded in the blistering heat without donkey or shadow.
moral: Quarreling over shadows loses both substance and peace.

Nasruddin dropped his stick, embraced his donkey around the neck, and apologized: "Forgive me, brother! You are the scholar, and I am the donkey!"
moral: Animals often possess more common sense than their impatient masters.

full_text:
Peering into his garden well at midnight, Nasruddin saw the radiant moon shining in the water: "Heavens! The moon has fallen into my well! I must rescue it!"

He tied a hook to a rope, tossed it into the well, and pulled. The hook caught on a submerged rock. Nasruddin pulled with all his might until the rope snapped, throwing him flat on his back on the grass.

Looking up into the night sky, he saw the full moon shining brightly above: "Praise be to heaven! It took a bruised spine and a broken rope, but I put the moon back in the sky where it belongs!"
moral: Mistaking a reflection for reality leads to unnecessary battles.

title: Nasruddin's House is Too Small
summary: A poor peasant came to Nasruddin complaining: "Mulla, my house is a misery! I, my wife, our four children, and my mother-in-law live in a single tiny room. We are crowded, noisy, a...
full_text:
A poor peasant came to Nasruddin complaining: "Mulla, my house is a misery! I, my wife, our four children, and my mother-in-law live in a single tiny room. We are crowded, noisy, and at each other's throats. Help me!"

Nasruddin advised: "Bring your six chickens into the room to live with you."

The man was horrified, but trusted the Mulla. A week later, he returned weeping: "It is unbearable! Chickens are flapping in our faces!"

"Bring in your two goats," commanded Nasruddin. A week later: "Bring in your donkey and cow!"

The following week, the man returned in tears of madness: "I cannot live! The house is a roaring zoo of dung and noise!"

Nasruddin smiled calmly: "Now go home, take out the cow, take out the donkey, take out the goats, and take out the chickens!"

The man ran home, cleared the animals, and returned the next morning, beaming with joy: "Mulla, God bless you! Our house is so vast, quiet, and peaceful! We live in a royal palace!"
moral: True contentment is discovered by recognizing how much worse things could be.

title: The Soup Stone

full_text:
During a severe winter, Nasruddin walked into a stingy village where no one would share food. He filled a cauldron with water, placed a smooth river stone inside, and set it on a fire in the town square.

"What are you making, Mulla?" asked a curious villager.

"I am cooking delicious Stone Soup!" smiled Nasruddin. "It is almost ready, though a handful of onions would make it fit for an emperor." A woman ran and brought onions.

"A few carrots and potatoes would crown its flavor," murmured Nasruddin. Another neighbor brought carrots and meat scraps.

Soon, the entire village sat together enjoying a steaming, rich communal feast—created by the magic of sharing.
moral: True sharing transforms a barren stone into a feast of community abundance.

Nasruddin loaded his donkey with heavy sacks of salt. While crossing a stream, the donkey slipped, and the salt dissolved in the water. Finding its load delightfully light, the cunning beast leaped out in joy.

The next day, the donkey deliberately tumbled into the stream again to dissolve the load.

Seeing through the trick, Nasruddin loaded the donkey with large bales of dry sponges the following morning.

When the donkey plunged into the river, the sponges absorbed gallons of water, multiplying the weight fivefold! The drenched animal barely managed to crawl ashore, cured forever of playing tricks.
moral: Tricks that seek to shirk duty eventually turn into heavier burdens.

moral: The greed of extortionists is insatiable; words cannot satisfy what demands all.

His wife wished for a necklace of pearls; in anger at her greed, Nasruddin wished the pearls were stuck to her nose. Regretting his temper, he had to use his third wish to take the pearls off her nose!

"You see?" smiled Nasruddin. "We have gained nothing, lost nothing, and learned that wishing for more only leads to an aching nose!"
moral: Reckless wishes waste miraculous opportunities; contentment is the true wish.

Accused of stealing a lost camel because he accurately described it as blind in one eye, lame in one leg, and carrying honey and wheat, Nasruddin explained:

"I saw that the grass was eaten only on one side of the trail—hence blind in one eye; the tracks showed three deep prints and one dragging—hence lame; ants swarmed on one side of the road for fallen wheat, and flies swarmed on the other for honey! I never saw the beast!" The judge dismissed the charges in admiration.
moral: Careful observation of small tracks reveals the entire truth.

full_text:
A neighbor asked Nasruddin: "Mulla, I hear you have a jar of forty-year-old balsamic vinegar. Please give me a spoonful to cure my wife's cough!"

"I cannot give you any," replied Nasruddin.

"Why not?" asked the neighbor.

"Because," said Nasruddin, "if I had given spoonfuls away to everyone who asked, it would never have lasted forty years!"
moral: A miser's treasure is useless so long as it remains locked away from human need.

title: Nasruddin's Age (The Consistent Sage)
summary: When asked his age, Nasruddin replied: "I am forty years old."...

When asked his age, Nasruddin replied: "I am forty years old."

"Mulla," cried the clerk, "you said you were forty years old ten years ago!"

"Of course!" said Nasruddin. "A true gentleman stands by his word; I am not a fickle man who changes his age with every passing breeze!"
moral: Consistency in words is a virtue, even when calendars disagree.

summary: Nasruddin was leading his donkey to the bazaar. A passerby said: "Mulla, that donkey's tail is much too long; it looks untidy!" Nasruddin took his shears and snipped off half the t...
full_text:
Nasruddin was leading his donkey to the bazaar. A passerby said: "Mulla, that donkey's tail is much too long; it looks untidy!" Nasruddin took his shears and snipped off half the tail.

A little further, an old woman scolded: "Shame on you! You cut the poor beast's tail so short it cannot brush away the flies!" Nasruddin tried to tie the severed hairs back on.

Another man laughed: "Look at that ridiculous patchwork tail!"

Nasruddin threw his hands in the air: "If a man listens to every fool in the marketplace, he will end up cutting off his own ears to please the crowd!"
moral: Trying to please every critic in the crowd leads only to losing one's head.

title: Nasruddin and the Orchard
summary: Nasruddin climbed over a high wall into an orchard to eat sweet figs. The owner suddenly appeared with an iron pitchfork: "What are you doing up in my fig tree, thief?"...
full_text:
Nasruddin climbed over a high wall into an orchard to eat sweet figs. The owner suddenly appeared with an iron pitchfork: "What are you doing up in my fig tree, thief?"

Nasruddin sang: "Tweet, tweet! Trill, trill!"

"What kind of noise is that?" roared the furious gardener.

"I am a nightingale!" replied Nasruddin.

"A nightingale?" shouted the man. "I have never heard such a coarse, discordant song!"

"Well," said Nasruddin calmly, "that is because I am only an amateur nightingale who is still taking singing lessons!" The gardener laughed and handed him a basket of figs.
moral: When caught in error, quick wit softens anger and opens the door to laughter.

"What are you doing?" asked the bewildered fisherman.

"Saving this poor creature from drowning in the river!" replied Nasruddin proudly.
moral: Misguided empathy often does more harm than honest understanding.

title: The Blind Man's Lamp

full_text:
Nasruddin met a blind man walking through the dark streets at midnight, carrying a heavy earthen water jar on his shoulder and a brightly burning lantern in his hand.

Nasruddin asked: "My friend, you are blind and day and night are the same to you; why do you carry a burning lamp?"

The blind man smiled: "I carry the lamp not that I may see where I am going, but so that careless people with eyes may not bump into me and break my water jar!"

Nasruddin bowed with deep respect, realizing that the blind man saw more clearly than those with sight.
moral: True courtesy thinks of the blindness of others.

A notoriously bad neighbor asked to borrow Nasruddin's long clothesline.

Nasruddin went inside and returned saying: "I am sorry, neighbor, but I cannot lend you my rope today; my wife is currently spreading flour across it to dry in the sun."

"Spreading flour on a rope?" gasped the neighbor. "How can anyone spread flour on a thin rope?"

"My dear neighbor," smiled Nasruddin, "when one does not wish to lend his rope, it is astonishing how easily flour can be spread upon it!"
moral: An absurd refusal is the best answer to an unreasonable demand.

title: Nasruddin and the Eagle

"Heavens!" cried Nasruddin. "What a neglected bird! Your beak is curved like a sickle, your claws are sharp as needles, and your feathers are wild and unruly!"

He took large shears, trimmed the eagle's magnificent hooked beak straight, cut its mighty talons blunt, and combed its feathers flat.

He stroked the bird with satisfaction: "There now! You look like a proper, respectable domestic pigeon!"
moral: Forcing wild magnificence into ordinary domestic molds destroys its beauty.

title: Nasruddin and the Elephant
summary: Timur the Conqueror left his giant imperial war elephant in Nasruddin's village. The ravenous beast trampled orchards, drank entire cisterns, and devastated the peasants' crops....
full_text:
Timur the Conqueror left his giant imperial war elephant in Nasruddin's village. The ravenous beast trampled orchards, drank entire cisterns, and devastated the peasants' crops.

The terrified villagers begged Nasruddin: "Lead us before Timur! We will stand behind you and demand he remove the elephant!"

Nasruddin led thirty villagers to Timur's royal tent. But when Timur roared: "What do you want, peasants?", Nasruddin turned around and saw that every single villager had fled in terror, leaving him standing completely alone!

Nasruddin smiled with serene composure: "Sire! The villagers sent me to express our boundless gratitude for your magnificent elephant! We are so enchanted with the noble beast that we humbly beg you to send a female elephant to keep him company!"

Timur was delighted and sent a second elephant, teaching the cowardly villagers a bitter lesson about solidarity.
moral: Fair-weather friends flee when danger arrives; face trials with those who stand firm.

moral: If the world will not bend to your pride, bend yourself in humble flexibility.

title: The Donkey in the Well (The Art of Stepping Up)
summary: Nasruddin's old donkey fell into an abandoned dry well. Unable to pull the heavy animal out, the villagers decided to bury the well with shovels of dirt to put it out of its misery...
keywords: the donkey in the well - wisdom
full_text:
Nasruddin's old donkey fell into an abandoned dry well. Unable to pull the heavy animal out, the villagers decided to bury the well with shovels of dirt to put it out of its misery.

As shovelfuls of earth rained down upon its back, the donkey cried out in distress. But soon it quieted down.

With every shovel of dirt that struck its back, the donkey shook the earth off and stepped upward on top of it!

Shovel by shovel, step by step, the earth piled higher beneath its hooves until, to the astonishment of the crowd, the triumphant beast stepped proudly out over the lip of the well and trotted away to graze!

Nasruddin smiled: "Life throws dirt upon your shoulders; do not let it bury you! Shake it off and step up!"
moral: Shake off the dirt cast upon you and use every hardship as a stepping stone.

When a hungry wolf blocked the path of Nasruddin's donkey, the clever beast began limping, crying: "Brother wolf, pull the sharp thorn from my hind hoof before you eat me, so it does not pierce your throat!"

When the wolf bent to inspect the hoof, the donkey kicked him in the jaw with both hooves, knocking out his teeth, and trotted safely home with Nasruddin!
moral: Presence of mind in deadly peril saves life when flight is impossible.

moral: A flame shared with another loses none of its own brilliance.

A banquet guest ate seven bowls of pilaf, three roast chickens, and twenty pastries until he collapsed groaning on the cushions.

moral: Gluttony turns festive feasts into chambers of digestive regret.

title: Nasruddin and the Goose (The One-Legged Marvel)
summary: Nasruddin roasted a fat goose as a present for Timur. On the road, growing famished, he ate one of the drumsticks....
full_text:
Nasruddin roasted a fat goose as a present for Timur. On the road, growing famished, he ate one of the drumsticks.

When Timur saw the bird on the golden platter, he demanded angrily: "Where is the other leg of this goose?"

Nasruddin pointed out the window to a flock of geese resting near the pond, each standing asleep on a single leg: "Sire, all the geese in this province have only one leg!"

Timur clapped his hands loudly: "Shoo! Shoo!"

The geese startled, put down their other legs, and ran across the grass.

Timur glared at Nasruddin: "Look, fool! They have two legs!"

"Ah, Sire!" replied Nasruddin with deep bow. "If you clapped your hands at a man as loudly as you did at those birds, he would run away on four legs!" Timur laughed and rewarded him.
moral: Quick wit disarms tyrannical wrath with laughter.

title: Nasruddin's Mother-in-Law
summary: Nasruddin's notoriously contrary mother-in-law fell into a rushing mountain river and was swept away....
full_text:
Nasruddin's notoriously contrary mother-in-law fell into a rushing mountain river and was swept away.

The villagers ran downstream with ropes to search for her body.

Nasruddin ran with all his might upstream toward the mountain source!

"Mulla!" shouted the searchers. "The river flows down; why do you search upstream?"

"You don't know my mother-in-law!" gasped Nasruddin. "She was so contrary in everything she did in life that she would surely float against the current!"
moral: Habits of stubborn contradiction become second nature even in the current of death.

moral: Greed that attempts to monetize what God created free earns empty pockets.

title: Nasruddin and the Beggar

full_text:
A beggar knocked at Nasruddin's street door. Nasruddin, who was resting in his second-story study, leaned out: "What do you want?"

"Come down, master, I have an urgent matter!" called the beggar.

Nasruddin climbed all the way down the long flight of stairs to the door. "What is it?"

"Give me a copper coin for bread," whispered the beggar.

Nasruddin looked at him: "Follow me upstairs." The beggar climbed the stairs with high hopes. In the study, Nasruddin turned to him: "I have no money for you."

"Why didn't you tell me that downstairs?" complained the beggar.

"Why did you call me all the way downstairs merely to ask for money?" replied Nasruddin.
moral: Do not demand that others climb mountains merely to hear a refusal.

title: The Man Who Wanted to Be a King

A dissatisfied farmer said: "Mulla, I wish I were a king with a golden crown and ten thousand soldiers!"

Nasruddin placed an iron cooking pot on the man's head and handed him a heavy log: "Wear this pot for three hours without moving, and stand guard against imaginary assassins!"

Within thirty minutes, the man's neck ached and he begged for release.

"You see?" smiled Nasruddin. "A crown is heavy, guards bring suspicion, and fear haunts the throne. Eat your bread in freedom and sleep in peace!"
moral: A peasant who sleeps in peace is freer than a crowned monarch besieged by fear.

Nasruddin pointed to the heavy door on his back: "Mother, you told me to watch the door, not the house! The door has not left my sight for a single second!"

title: Nasruddin Tale 167: The Walnut and the Pumpkin
summary: Nasruddin rested beneath the shade of an enormous walnut tree beside a patch of giant pumpkins....
full_text:
Nasruddin rested beneath the shade of an enormous walnut tree beside a patch of giant pumpkins.

He pondered: "How strange is creation! Heavy pumpkins weighing twenty pounds grow on frail, crawling vines on the ground; while tiny walnuts grow on majestic, towering branches! Surely I could have arranged nature with far greater wisdom!"

Just then, a sudden breeze shook the boughs, and a heavy walnut fell straight from the high branch, striking Nasruddin squarely on the forehead!

Nasruddin rubbed his bruised brow, prostrated himself on the grass, and prayed: "Forgive my arrogant meddling, O Creator! For if giant twenty-pound pumpkins grew on high branches, my head would have been smashed to pieces this day!"
moral: Questioning divine creation often results in a walnut falling on your head.

title: Nasruddin Tale 171: The Midnight Noise
summary: In the middle of the night, a tremendous crash and clatter echoed from Nasruddin's house, shaking the walls and waking the entire lane....
full_text:
In the middle of the night, a tremendous crash and clatter echoed from Nasruddin's house, shaking the walls and waking the entire lane.

A terrified neighbor pounded on the door: "Mulla, what on earth was that terrifying crash?"

"It was nothing," replied Nasruddin through the window. "My woolen shirt fell down the wooden stairs."

"Certainly," sighed Nasruddin, "when I am inside the shirt when it tumbles down the stairs!"

title: Nasruddin Tale 172: The Hot Bread

full_text:
Nasruddin pulled a loaf of fresh flatbread from the baking oven and took a massive bite while it was still boiling hot. Burning his tongue and throat, he danced around the room, panting and fanning his mouth with both hands.

"Why don't you spit it out?" cried his wife.

"Spit out fresh bread?" gasped Nasruddin. "Never! I would rather let my tongue burn than let honest bread go to waste!"
moral: Impatience burns the tongue; waiting for the right moment brings sweet digestion.

He swept the clay fragments into a neat pile, placed them around his rose bush to hold moisture in the soil, and took his wooden bowl to the spring, humming a cheerful tune of peace.
moral: Do not weep over what cannot be gathered; sweep the pieces and plant flowers.

title: Nasruddin Tale 175: The Sultan's Ring

full_text:
The Sultan asked Nasruddin to inscribe a motto on his royal signet ring that would make him humble in times of prosperity and comforted in times of sorrow.

Nasruddin had the jeweler carve four ancient words: "This Too Shall Pass."

The Sultan wept and embraced the sage, realizing that all earthly glory and sorrow are transient waves upon the eternal sea of time.
moral: In victory remain humble; in defeat remain hopeful; for this too shall pass.

title: Nasruddin Tale 176: The Two Halves of a Melon

"Because," smiled Nasruddin with a warm twinkle, "the half that brings a smile to your face is always the sweetest fruit in the house!"
moral: True affection shares sweetness without calculating advantage.

title: Nasruddin Tale 177: The Midnight Archer

full_text:
Waking in the dead of night, Nasruddin saw a white figure standing motionless in his garden. Suspecting a prowler, he grabbed his bow, notched an arrow, and shot the figure straight through the chest!

In the morning, he went out and found his own white nightshirt hanging on the clothesline, with an arrow through the middle.

Nasruddin prostrated on the lawn in prayer: "Praise be to heaven! What a miracle that I was not wearing my nightshirt when I shot it, or I would have killed myself with my own arrow!"
moral: Find gratitude in every narrow escape, even when the arrow is your own.

moral: A diamond trampled in dust is still a gem; mud upon a prince does not taint his soul.

moral: We plant trees not for ourselves alone, but so future generations may harvest peace.

title: Nasruddin Tale 180: The Beggar and the Emperor

Timur asked Nasruddin: "If I were to sell you as a slave in the market, what would you fetch?"

"Thirty copper coins," replied Nasruddin.

"Insolent fool!" roared Timur. "The silk sash around my waist alone is worth thirty coppers!"

"Exactly," smiled Nasruddin serenely. "I was estimating the value of the sash; the rest of you is worth nothing at all!" Timur laughed and spared his life.
moral: Before the grave, the emperor and the beggar share the same dust.

title: Nasruddin Tale 183: The Stolen Blanket

Hearing a violent brawl in the street late at night, Nasruddin wrapped his warm woolen blanket around his shoulders and ran out to make peace.

As soon as he stepped into the crowd, a rogue snatched the blanket off his back and ran away, and the other brawlers immediately dispersed!

Nasruddin walked back into his cold bedroom shivering.

"What was the quarrel about, husband?" asked his wife.

"It was about my blanket!" sighed Nasruddin. "As soon as they got it, the dispute ended completely!"
moral: Do not meddle in street brawls unless you are willing to lose your own blanket.

title: Nasruddin Tale 184: The Donkey and the Sack of Gold

full_text:
Nasruddin loaded his donkey with a sack of gold coins and a sack of fresh green clover.

He asked the animal: "Which sack do you prefer, brother: the one filled with royal gold, or the one filled with clover?"

The donkey buried its nose straight into the clover and munched happily.

Nasruddin nodded in admiration: "A creature of true discernment! He leaves cold bullion to greedy mortals and chooses what genuinely gives life."
moral: Gold is mere heavy stone to those who seek the nourishment of life.

moral: Truth reveals itself through natural instinct rather than fabricated perjury.

title: Nasruddin Tale 186: The Foreign Ambassador
summary: A foreign ambassador arrived who spoke only through signs. He drew a circle in the sand. Nasruddin drew a line across it. The ambassador held up three fingers; Nasruddin held up on...
full_text:
A foreign ambassador arrived who spoke only through signs. He drew a circle in the sand. Nasruddin drew a line across it. The ambassador held up three fingers; Nasruddin held up one. The ambassador held up an egg; Nasruddin held up an onion.

The ambassador bowed in deep awe: "Your scholar is a supreme genius! I showed him the earth; he showed me the equator! I showed him the three realms; he showed me divine unity! I showed him cosmic mystery; he showed me the layers of creation!"

After the envoy departed, the Sultan asked Nasruddin: "What did you say to him?"

Nasruddin laughed: "He showed me a round flatbread; I said I would cut it in half! He said he would eat three slices; I said I would eat the whole thing! Then he pulled out a boiled egg for lunch, and I showed him an onion to season it with!"
moral: Grand diplomatic gestures often conceal ordinary human appetites.

The miser refused to stretch out his hand, for in his entire life he had never given anything to anyone.

The miser immediately grabbed Nasruddin's hand and was pulled to safety.

Nasruddin explained: "He has never learned the word 'give,' but he understands the word 'take' perfectly!"
moral: To reach a miser, speak the language of receiving rather than giving.

title: Nasruddin Tale 197: The Honeycomb
summary: Showing a honeycomb to his students, Nasruddin remarked:...
full_text:
Showing a honeycomb to his students, Nasruddin remarked:

"Ten thousand bees gather nectar from a million blossoms, and each contributes a single drop to build this golden comb. Learn from the bees: unity, industry, and sweet speech turn bitter lives into golden honey."
moral: The hive prospers when every bee contributes honey to the comb.

title: Nasruddin Tale 198: The Two Beggars at the Mosque
summary: Outside the mosque, one beggar flattered the rich worshippers, while the second beggar simply prayed: "O Lord, provide for Thy humble servant from Thy boundless bounty!"...
full_text:
Outside the mosque, one beggar flattered the rich worshippers, while the second beggar simply prayed: "O Lord, provide for Thy humble servant from Thy boundless bounty!"

A nobleman, seeking to test them, baked a pie filled with gold coins and gave it to the flatterer. The flatterer thought it was heavy and plain, and sold it to the second beggar for two coppers!

When the second beggar found the gold, he built an alms-house for orphans.

Nasruddin smiled: "He who looks to mortals receives crumbs; he who looks to heaven receives the treasure."
moral: True reliance on God receives boundless mercy; flattery receives mere pennies.

title: Nasruddin Tale 199: The King's Jester
summary: The King asked Nasruddin: "Who is the most indispensable officer in my empire?"...
full_text:
The King asked Nasruddin: "Who is the most indispensable officer in my empire?"

"Your court jester, Sire!" replied Nasruddin. "Your ministers tell you what will flatter your pride; your generals tell you what will wage wars; but your jester is the only man who tells you the unvarnished truth while making you laugh!"
moral: The jester who tells truth at court is wiser than a council of yes-men.

title: Nasruddin Tale 200: The Locked Gate with No Walls
summary: In his final years in the town of Aksehir, Mulla Nasruddin designed his own tomb....
full_text:
In his final years in the town of Aksehir, Mulla Nasruddin designed his own tomb.

He built a magnificent iron gate, fitted with a gigantic, heavy brass padlock that could never be opened. But around the gate, there were no walls, no fences, and no barriers whatsoever—the open green fields stretched freely on every side!

Travelers came from across the world and asked in bewilderment: "Why is there an enormous locked gate with no walls? Anyone can simply walk around it!"

Nasruddin's ghost chuckled from the eternal meadows: "That is the supreme riddle of human existence! Mortals spend their lives beating their heads against locked gates of dogma, fear, and pride, blind to the fact that the walls never existed, and that freedom and truth surround them on every side!"
moral: The gates of illusion are locked with heavy padlocks, yet the walls never existed at all.
